ledger.note: The workflow checks out the PR head sha and runs npm test, which runs PR-controlled package.json scripts and test files, with the secret in env.

ledger.unit: Router error handling / body parsing | any client -> internal details / resources | info leak, DoS
ledger.note: Only errors marked expose return their messages, otherwise the response is 'internal error'. The body is capped at 1MB. The body is parsed before auth, which is a hardening note only.

items.title: Cross-tenant note read via GET /notes/:id
items.boundary: member of tenant t1 -> per-tenant isolation (README) -> notes of tenant t2
items.reason: The handler returns notes.get(id) with no comparison of note.tenantId to req.user.tenantId. The sibling PUT does make that comparison (line 14), and the list filters by tenant (line 6). As u1 (t1), GET /notes/n2 returns tenant t2's note body.

items.title: Path traversal in export name escapes tenant directory
items.boundary: member of tenant t1 -> tenant-scoped export directory -> other tenants' .csv exports and any readable *.csv on the server filesystem
items.reason: name comes from the query string (URLSearchParams decodes it) and is only required to end in '.csv'. path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, name) resolves '../t2/x.csv' or '../../../x.csv' outside the tenant dir, and there is no containment check, unlike avatars.mjs:11. The file contents are returned. Which files exist is runtime state, but no control blocks the read.

items.title: fetch_doc URL allowlist bypass by string prefix (SSRF)
items.boundary: signed-in member (or assistant-chosen args) -> docs.example.com egress allowlist -> arbitrary https hosts reachable from the server, with the response read back
items.reason: String(url).startsWith('https://docs.example.com') accepts 'https://docs.example.com.attacker.tld/' and 'https://docs.example.com@10.0.0.5/' (userinfo form). redirect:'error' blocks only redirects, not the initial host, and up to 20000 chars of the body are returned to the caller. The member can supply args directly in the request body. What internal https services exist is deployment-dependent; the allowlist bypass and the read-back are fully source-visible.

items.title: pull_request_target executes PR head code with PREVIEW_DEPLOY_TOKEN
items.boundary: external PR author -> base-repo workflow trust (secrets) -> PREVIEW_DEPLOY_TOKEN
items.reason: pull_request_target runs with base-repo secrets on opened/synchronize. The checkout uses github.event.pull_request.head.sha, and npm test then runs the PR's own package.json script and test/ files with the secret in env. Any PR author can print or exfiltrate it. permissions: contents: read limits only GITHUB_TOKEN, not the secret, and the workflow has no gating (labels, environment approval).

items.title: X-Impersonate-User grants any identity including admin when enabled
items.boundary: unauthenticated network client -> bearer authentication / requireAdmin -> any member's tenant data and /admin tenant deletion
items.reason: When the flag is on, the header value alone selects the user. There is no secret, loopback/IP restriction or support-role check, so 'x-impersonate-user: ops1' passes requireAdmin. Unresolved fact: whether any deployment reachable by untrusted clients runs with SUPPORT_IMPERSONATION=on. Source sets it only in docker-compose.dev.yml, which publishes 8080:8080 on all host interfaces (not localhost-only), despite the README framing it as local debugging.

items.title: Signed payment webhook can be replayed to re-credit balance
items.boundary: party holding a previously valid signed webhook request -> provider signature (authenticity/freshness) -> account balances
items.reason: x-signature-timestamp is included in the HMAC but never compared to the current time, and there is no event-id dedup. Resending an identical signed request credits the amount again. Unresolved fact: whether a lower-trust party can obtain a previously signed request (e.g. via logs, a proxy, or provider retry delivery). Forging a new event is not possible from source.

items.title: Avatar name traversal
items.boundary: authenticated member -> AVATAR_ROOT containment -> server filesystem
items.reason: Refuted by path.resolve(AVATAR_ROOT, name) plus startsWith(AVATAR_ROOT + path.sep), which rejects decoded '../' and absolute names. Avatars being cross-tenant is intended (README:7).

items.title: SQL injection via sort/dir/q
items.boundary: member -> parameterized query -> notes table of other tenants
items.reason: Refuted: the interpolated column is restricted to the SORTABLE allowlist, the direction is a fixed literal, and the user q and tenant_id are bound $1/$2 params.

items.title: Reaching /admin without admin role
items.boundary: member -> requireAdmin -> tenant management
items.reason: Refuted for the bearer path: the chain runs authenticate and then requireAdmin, and prefix matching is exact or 'prefix/'. Members have role 'member'. The only bypass is the impersonation item above.

items.title: Session token forgery or expiry bypass
items.boundary: unauthenticated client -> HMAC session token -> any user
items.reason: Refuted: the HMAC-SHA256 signature is verified in constant time with a length check before the claims are parsed, and exp is enforced.

items.title: Forging payment webhook
items.boundary: unauthenticated network -> webhook HMAC -> balances
items.reason: Refuted: requests are rejected when the secret is empty, and the HMAC over the raw body is checked with timingSafeEqual and a length check.

items.title: Tool dispatch prototype lookup / list_notes cross-tenant
items.boundary: member -> tool allowlist / tenant filter -> other tools or tenants' notes
items.reason: Refuted: Object.hasOwn blocks inherited names, and list_notes filters by user.tenantId.

hardening: SESSION_SECRET falls back to random bytes (src/auth.mjs:4). Tokens are invalidated on restart and differ between instances, so an explicit secret should be required.
The request body is read and JSON-parsed (up to 1MB) for every request before authentication (src/router.mjs:18). Consider auth-first parsing or a lower limit.
actions/checkout persists GITHUB_TOKEN in .git/config by default. Set persist-credentials: false and pin actions to commit SHAs (.github/workflows/pr.yml:11,14).
Webhook: no validation of event.amount sign/finiteness (src/webhooks.mjs:18). It relies entirely on the provider's signature.
fetch_doc returns 500 on network errors versus 200 with a body, a minor reachability oracle. Parse with new URL() and compare origin/hostname exactly.
Avatars: the containment check does not resolve symlinks inside AVATAR_ROOT, so use realpath if writable by others. Avatars require auth even though README calls them public (no security impact).
The admin principal (tenantId null) on tenant routes maps to the 'null' export directory. Consider rejecting tenantless users explicitly on tenant routes.

ab0b2dbc.reason: Every trace location exists and matches the description. src/server.mjs:14 mounts /notes behind authenticate only, with no requireAdmin or tenant middleware. src/auth.mjs:26-35 only establishes identity: a valid HMAC bearer token is mapped to a user via users.get(sub) and nothing tenant-related is checked. src/router.mjs:41 (match) puts the ':id' path segment, URL-decoded, into req.params, and Router.handle applies no other normalization or authorization. In src/routes/notes.mjs, line 7 is the GET '/:id' route, line 8 is notes.get(req.params.id), and line 10 returns the whole note object, including tenantId, ownerId, title and body. Nothing compares note.tenantId with req.user.tenantId on this path. That comparison exists only in PUT (line 14), and the list route filters by tenant (line 6), which shows the isolation was intended. README line 5 states that members may only read data of their own tenant. src/db.mjs gives the concrete case: u1 is a member of t1, and n2 belongs to t2 with body 'tenant two note'. So u1, holding a legitimately issued token, can send GET /notes/n2 and receive tenant t2's note with status 200. The claimed effect, reading another tenant's note, is exactly what the code shows and is not overstated. The only prerequisite is an ordinary authenticated member session, which is the lower-trust actor in the boundary.

adaf4d0d.reason: Every trace location exists and matches the description. server.mjs:15 mounts /export behind `authenticate` only; that check needs a valid HMAC Bearer token and sets req.user from db.users. There is no per-route tenant authorization. router.mjs:16-17 decodes the query with URLSearchParams into req.query, so `?name=../t2/x.csv` (or the %2e%2e%2f form) reaches the handler as a raw string. For GET /export, req.path is '/', which matches the route. export.mjs:10-11 applies only one check: `name.endsWith('.csv')`. export.mjs:12 calls `path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, name)`, which normalizes the '..' segments and resolves to EXPORT_ROOT/t2/x.csv, or further up with more '../'. No resolve-plus-startsWith containment check follows, unlike avatars.mjs:10-11. export.mjs:13 reads the file as utf8 and export.mjs:15 returns its contents in the JSON response. README states that each member may only read data of their own tenant, so reading t2's export is a real cross-tenant boundary break. Impact is limited to files whose path ends in '.csv' that the process can read: a NUL-byte suffix bypass is not possible because fs rejects NUL in paths. Within that limit, both other tenants' exports and arbitrary readable *.csv files on the host are reachable. Which .csv files actually exist depends on the deployment, but that does not change whether the read primitive exists.

a60f9a31.reason: The trace locations exist and match. server.mjs:18 mounts /agent behind authenticate, and any signed-in member can POST /agent/tool-call with {name:'fetch_doc',args:{url}} (routes.mjs:7-9). tools.mjs:7 checks the URL only with String(url).startsWith('https://docs.example.com'). tools.mjs:10-11 fetches it with redirect:'error' and returns up to 20000 chars. So the prefix check is weak, but source does not support the claimed effect of arbitrary HTTPS hosts reachable from the server, with the response read back. (1) The userinfo form 'https://docs.example.com@10.0.0.5/' does not work: Node 22's global fetch (node:22-alpine in docker-compose.dev.yml) follows the Fetch spec and throws a TypeError for a URL that includes credentials, so no request is sent. (2) The 'https://docs.example.com.attacker.tld/' form (also 'docs.example.comX.tld' or adding a port) only reaches hostnames the attacker controls. The scheme is forced to https and TLS certificate checks stay on, because no NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, custom agent or dispatcher appears anywhere in source or compose. So pointing attacker DNS at an internal IP fails the hostname check against the internal service's certificate, and redirect:'error' blocks the redirect pivot. What is left is the server fetching attacker-owned content and returning it to the same attacker. That content is already available to them, and the step crosses no meaningful confidentiality or integrity boundary. The bypass is still worth hardening (parse with new URL and compare the hostname exactly), but the SSRF impact claimed is not established and is blocked by visible runtime controls.

a0429e70.reason: I could not refute the candidate from the source. Every trace location exists and says what the candidate claims. pr.yml:3 triggers on pull_request_target for opened and synchronize (lines 3-4). That event runs in the base repo's context, so the job can read base-repo secrets, and PRs from forks trigger it. pr.yml:13 checks out ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}, which is code the PR author controls. pr.yml:17 runs `npm test` with PREVIEW_DEPLOY_TOKEN set from secrets.PREVIEW_DEPLOY_TOKEN (line 19). package.json:5 defines test as `node --test test/`. Both package.json and the test/ files come from the PR head, so an external author can rewrite the script or add a test file and run any code that reads the token from the environment. I found no control in the source that blocks this. There is no `if:` condition on author or labels, no `environment:` (so no required-reviewer gate), no separate trusted and untrusted jobs, no persist-credentials setting, and no other workflow files in the repo. `permissions: contents: read` only limits GITHUB_TOKEN. It does not restrict repository secrets. The README and src/ add nothing that gates the workflow. The claimed impact is that PR-author code runs with PREVIEW_DEPLOY_TOKEN available and can take it, and the source establishes that fully. What the token can do once taken is not shown in the source, but the candidate does not claim more than exposure of the secret.

a414c52f.reason: I could not refute the trace from source. Each listed location exists and does what the candidate says. src/server.mjs:14 and :19 mount authenticate on /notes and authenticate+requireAdmin on /admin. src/auth.mjs:27-28: when process.env.SUPPORT_IMPERSONATION === 'on' and an x-impersonate-user header is present, req.user = users.get(header) with no token, signature, caller-role, loopback or NODE_ENV check, and the else branch holding the bearer/HMAC verify is skipped entirely. src/auth.mjs:38 requireAdmin only checks req.user.role === 'admin'. src/db.mjs:4 seeds ops1 with role 'admin', so 'x-impersonate-user: ops1' passes. src/routes/admin.mjs:7-10 DELETE /admin/tenants/:id deletes the tenant and all its notes. Naming u1 or u2 likewise gives that member's identity on /notes and the other authenticated mounts. src/router.mjs adds no auth or header filtering. Searching the repo shows the flag is enabled only in docker-compose.dev.yml:8. That file also maps ports 8080:8080, which is all interfaces by default. README.md:8 calls the feature 'for local debugging'. No production or deployment configuration exists in source, and the CI workflow (.github/workflows/pr.yml) only runs npm test. The bypass is therefore fully established when the flag is on. Whether it reaches an untrusted client depends on deployment environment, which source does not contain.
a414c52f.unresolved_fact: Whether any deployment reachable by untrusted network clients (production, staging, or a dev host whose published 0.0.0.0:8080 is network-exposed) runs the service with SUPPORT_IMPERSONATION=on. Source sets it only in docker-compose.dev.yml and has no production deployment config.

a565ac5b.reason: I could not refute the trace from source, but source alone does not establish it either. Every trace location exists and matches. At src/server.mjs:13, /webhooks is mounted with no authenticate step. At src/webhooks.mjs:10-13 the handler reads x-signature-timestamp and x-signature, computes HMAC-SHA256(PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET, `${timestamp}.${rawBody}`), and rejects an empty secret or a length or timingSafeEqual mismatch. rawBody is the exact request bytes, captured in router.mjs readJson. That makes the signature check sound for authenticity, and an attacker cannot forge or change account or amount. Nowhere does the code compare the timestamp to Date.now(), and there is no event-id or nonce store; db.mjs only has the balances Map. So a byte-identical resend of a previously valid request passes again, and lines 17-18 add Number(event.amount) to the account again. This is a real cross-boundary effect: balances are credited more than once. The impact is limited to repeating credits the provider already signed, at the same account and amount. It is not arbitrary crediting. Exploiting it needs a party below the provider's trust level to hold a valid signed request (signature headers plus exact body), and nothing in the fixture logs, stores or exposes webhook headers or bodies. README.md only says the webhooks come from the payment provider. Getting such a request depends on infrastructure that is not in source.
a565ac5b.unresolved_fact: Whether a party below the provider's trust level can obtain a previously delivered, provider-signed webhook request (both the x-signature and x-signature-timestamp headers and the exact raw body). Possible routes: request logging at a reverse proxy or load balancer, an APM tool or log sink, the provider's dashboard or event-resend feature, TLS termination outside the app, or provider retry delivery. None of this is defined in the fixture source.

items.title: Cross-tenant invoice read via ?tenant= query override
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> tenant check in GET /invoices/:id -> invoices of tenant B
items.reason: GET /:id compares item.tenantId against (req.query.tenant ?? req.user.tenantId), so the client-supplied query value replaces the server-side tenant. A user of t2 requesting /invoices/<id>?tenant=t1 gets the t1 invoice. README line 5 says users may only read their own tenant's records. The other routes (list, PUT, DELETE) use req.user.tenantId or loadScoped, which shows this route departs from the shared control.

items.title: Report PUT lacks tenant scoping (cross-tenant edit by managers)
items.boundary: manager (or owner-id match) of tenant B -> tenant isolation in PUT /reports/:id -> reports of tenant A
items.reason: PUT uses store.get(req.params.id) instead of loadScoped, and its only check is `item.ownerId !== req.user.id && req.user.role !== 'manager'`. Manager m2 (tenant t2) therefore passes and can overwrite the title of any t1 report. README line 6 limits edits to a manager 'of the same tenant', and line 5 forbids changing other tenants' records. GET and DELETE in the same file use loadScoped.

items.title: Attachment DELETE has no tenant check
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> tenant check (loadScoped) missing in DELETE /attachments/:id -> attachments of tenant B
items.reason: DELETE calls store.delete(req.params.id) without first calling loadScoped(store, id, req.user), which every other resource's DELETE does. Any authenticated user who knows or obtains an attachment id from another tenant can delete it, and the 204 response does not reveal whether it existed. Ids are randomUUIDs (src/ids.mjs), so the attacker must know the id, but no authorization control exists.

items.title: Any same-tenant member can delete another user's report
items.boundary: non-owner member of tenant A -> owner/manager rule for reports -> reports of tenant A
items.reason: DELETE checks only the tenant (loadScoped) and has no owner/manager check, so u1 can delete a report owned by m1. Whether this is a violation depends on a fact the code does not settle: whether README line 6 ('a report may be edited only by its owner or by a manager') is meant to cover deletion. The product owner needs to confirm the intended authorization for DELETE /reports/:id.

items.title: Unscoped legacy-exports GET
items.boundary: authenticated user -> tenant check -> legacy-exports records
items.reason: The handler returns store.get(id) without a tenant check, but the module is neither imported nor mounted in src/registry.mjs (resources list lines 37-73), and server.mjs mounts only registry entries. The route cannot be reached. It is a latent risk if it is ever registered (see hardening).

items.title: Catalog returns all entries without tenant filter
items.boundary: authenticated user -> tenant filter -> catalog entries
items.reason: README line 7 defines /catalog as a global, read-only catalog shared by all tenants. The module defines only GET routes, so there is no write path.

items.title: Audit entry read uses an inline check instead of loadScoped
items.boundary: user of tenant A -> tenant check -> audit entries of tenant B
items.reason: The inline check `entry.tenantId !== req.user.tenantId` compares against the server-side user tenant, which is equivalent to loadScoped. The list is filtered the same way, and there are no write routes.

items.title: Unauthenticated access to resource routes
items.boundary: unauthenticated client -> authenticate middleware -> all resources
items.reason: Every registry mount is router.mount(prefix, authenticate, factory()). authenticate (auth.mjs:26-31) sends 401 unless an HMAC-valid, unexpired token maps to a known user. Router prefix matching (router.mjs:20) requires an exact match or prefix+'/', so no path bypasses this.

items.title: Token forgery / timing attack on signature
items.boundary: external client -> HMAC token verification -> user identity
items.reason: The signature is HMAC-SHA256 with a length check and crypto.timingSafeEqual. Claims are parsed only after the MAC is verified, and exp is enforced. Tenant and role come from the server-side users map (users.mjs), not from token claims.

items.title: Mass assignment of tenantId/ownerId via PUT/POST body
items.boundary: authenticated user -> field allowlist -> record tenant/owner
items.reason: All PUT handlers assign one named field coerced with String(). POST handlers build the item with tenantId/ownerId taken from req.user. No body spreading or Object.assign of the request body exists in any resource.

items.title: Internal error detail disclosure
items.boundary: external client -> error handler -> server internals
items.reason: Error messages are returned only when error.expose is set (on 404/413/400 errors created deliberately). Every other error returns the generic 'internal error'. A decodeURIComponent URIError at line 57 also ends up as a generic 500.

hardening: auth.mjs:4 falls back to a random per-process SESSION_SECRET. Whether production sets a strong, shared SESSION_SECRET is a deployment fact. No token issuance endpoint exists in the repo, so how sign() is exposed is outside the review scope.
Tokens have no revocation or audience claims, and authenticate does not catch a malformed-claims JSON.parse error (reachable only with a valid MAC, so it ends up as a 500, not a bypass).

router.mjs:18 reads and parses the body (up to 1 MB) before authentication and has no request timeout. Consider authenticating before reading the body and adding timeouts to limit unauthenticated resource use.
legacy-exports.mjs is dead code with an unscoped GET. Delete it, or switch it to loadScoped before it is ever added to registry.mjs.

Route handlers implement tenant checks inconsistently (inline checks, loadScoped, or none). Enforcing loadScoped centrally for every :id route, and adding tests for cross-tenant GET/PUT/DELETE per resource, would catch regressions like those in invoices, reports and attachments. The only existing test (test/scoped.test.mjs) covers just the loadScoped helper.
No tests or fixture code were executed. All verdicts rest on static source evidence only.

items.title: DELETE /attachments/:id removes records of any tenant
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> tenant scoping (loadScoped) omitted on DELETE -> tenant B attachment records
items.reason: The DELETE handler (lines 16-19) calls store.delete(req.params.id) with no loadScoped or tenantId check. Every other mutating handler in this file and its sibling resources calls loadScoped first. Any authenticated user who knows or obtains an id can delete another tenant's attachment and gets 204. This breaks the README rule that users may only change records of their own tenant.

items.title: GET /invoices/:id tenant taken from ?tenant query
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> tenant check compares against client-supplied req.query.tenant instead of req.user.tenantId -> tenant B invoice data
items.reason: The tenant check is item.tenantId !== (req.query.tenant ?? req.user.tenantId). req.query is built from URL searchParams in router.mjs:16 without validation, so GET /invoices/<id>?tenant=t2 returns a t2 invoice to a t1 user. This breaks the README's own-tenant-only read rule. The list, PUT and DELETE handlers correctly use loadScoped and req.user.

items.title: PUT /reports/:id missing tenant check; managers can edit other tenants' reports
items.boundary: manager of tenant B (or any user probing ids) -> PUT uses store.get without loadScoped; role check ignores tenant -> tenant A reports (integrity), plus an existence oracle via 403 vs 404
items.reason: Lines 12-14 load the item with store.get and allow the write when ownerId===req.user.id or req.user.role==='manager'. There is no item.tenantId===req.user.tenantId check, so m2 (tenant t2, users.mjs) can change the title of a t1 report. The README allows only the owner or a manager *of the same tenant*. Non-managers in other tenants get 403 instead of 404, which shows that a foreign id exists.

items.title: Unscoped GET /legacy-exports/:id
items.boundary: authenticated user -> no tenant check -> legacy-exports records
items.reason: The handler does lack a tenant check. However, the module is not imported or listed in src/registry.mjs, and server.mjs mounts only the registry's resources, so the route cannot be reached through any HTTP path. This is dead code that contradicts README line 8; it is listed under hardening.

items.title: Catalog lists and reads without tenant filter
items.boundary: authenticated user of any tenant -> no tenant filter -> catalog entries
items.reason: The README defines /catalog as a global, read-only product catalog shared by all tenants. Only GET routes exist, so there is no write path.

items.title: Audit read uses an inline tenant check instead of loadScoped
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> audit GET -> tenant B audit entries
items.reason: The list (line 9) and get (line 12) both compare entry.tenantId with req.user.tenantId and return 404 on a mismatch. There are no write routes.

items.title: Possible unauthenticated route reachability or prefix confusion
items.boundary: unauthenticated client -> authenticate middleware -> all resources
items.reason: server.mjs:8 mounts every registry prefix with authenticate first in the chain. The prefix match requires an exact match or prefix+'/' (so /catalogx does not match /catalog). Unmatched paths return 404 before any handler runs.

items.title: Token forgery or expiry bypass
items.boundary: unauthenticated client -> HMAC token verification -> user identity
items.reason: The HMAC-SHA256 is compared with timingSafeEqual after a length check, exp is required to be a number and must not have passed, and sub is resolved through the users Map. A malformed body after a valid MAC cannot be produced without SECRET.

items.title: Other template resources (accounts...timesheets) cross-tenant access
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant A -> loadScoped -> tenant B records
items.reason: All remaining resources follow the same pattern: GET/PUT/DELETE by id go through loadScoped (scoped.mjs compares tenantId and returns 404), lists filter by req.user.tenantId, POST takes tenantId and ownerId from req.user, and only a single String-coerced field is assigned (no mass assignment).

items.title: Random SESSION_SECRET fallback
items.boundary: token holder -> session secret configuration -> session validity across instances and restarts
items.reason: Unresolved fact: whether production deployments always set SESSION_SECRET. Without it, each process generates its own secret, so tokens fail across replicas and restarts. That is an availability and operations problem rather than a boundary bypass, and the deployment configuration is not in the repository.

hardening: router.mjs reads and JSON-parses up to 1 MB of request body before authentication runs; consider authenticating first or lowering the limit for unauthenticated requests.
auth.mjs verify() calls JSON.parse on the token body without try/catch; malformed input after a valid MAC is not realistically reachable, but wrapping it would return 401 instead of 500.
router.mjs match() calls decodeURIComponent on path segments; malformed percent-encoding throws URIError and returns 500 instead of 400.
Delete or register-and-scope src/resources/legacy-exports.mjs so it cannot later be mounted without a tenant check (it also contradicts README line 8).

Centralize tenant scoping (for example in a shared CRUD factory) so per-handler omissions like attachments DELETE, invoices GET and reports PUT cannot recur; add per-route cross-tenant tests, since test/scoped.test.mjs only covers loadScoped itself.
Tokens have no revocation; a user removed from the users map is rejected, but role changes take effect only through the map lookup, which is acceptable as is.

items.title: Report PUT skips tenant check; any manager can edit other tenants' reports
items.boundary: manager of tenant B -> tenant isolation (loadScoped not used) -> tenant A report records
items.reason: PUT /reports/:id uses store.get(req.params.id) and only checks `item.ownerId !== req.user.id && req.user.role !== 'manager'` (line 14). It never compares item.tenantId with req.user.tenantId, unlike every other handler, which calls loadScoped (src/scoped.mjs:3). So m2 (t2, manager in src/users.mjs) passes the check for any t1 report and overwrites its title (line 15). README lines 5-6 say a manager may edit only reports of the same tenant. The different status codes (404 vs 403) also tell a member of another tenant whether a report id exists.

items.title: Invoice GET lets the caller choose the tenant with ?tenant=
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant B -> tenant isolation (query parameter overrides session tenant) -> tenant A invoice records
items.reason: The handler compares item.tenantId against `req.query.tenant ?? req.user.tenantId`. req.query comes straight from the URL (src/router.mjs:17), so GET /invoices/<id>?tenant=t1 by u2 returns a t1 invoice. README line 5 says users may only read records of their own tenant. The list route and PUT/DELETE correctly use req.user.tenantId and loadScoped.

items.title: Attachment DELETE has no tenant check
items.boundary: authenticated user of tenant B -> tenant isolation (missing loadScoped) -> tenant A attachment records
items.reason: DELETE /attachments/:id calls store.delete(req.params.id) without loadScoped, whereas GET and PUT in the same file (lines 10 and 12) and DELETE in every other resource scope by tenant. Any authenticated user who has an attachment id can delete another tenant's attachment, and the 204 response does not depend on whether the record exists. UUID ids (src/ids.mjs) make ids hard to guess but are not an authorization control.

items.title: Report DELETE has no owner/manager check
items.boundary: non-owner member of the same tenant -> report owner/manager rule -> report records
items.reason: DELETE uses only loadScoped, which checks the tenant, so any same-tenant member can delete a report they cannot edit through PUT. README line 6 limits 'edited' to the owner or a manager but does not say whether deletion counts as editing. Unresolved fact: whether the product specification treats deleting a report as an edit that the owner/manager rule restricts.

items.title: legacy-exports GET has no tenant check

a11f5d24.reason: The trace locations are real. src/server.mjs:7 mounts every resource behind authenticate. src/auth.mjs:29 resolves req.user from an HMAC-verified token. src/resources/attachments.mjs:16-19 handles DELETE /:id by calling store.delete(req.params.id) without loadScoped, unlike GET and PUT in the same file and the DELETE handlers in assets.mjs and comments.mjs. A grep of src/ and test/ finds no other module that calls storeFor('attachments') or writes to that Map, and there is no seeding or persistence layer. aaede1d9.reason: Every trace location exists and matches the claim. src/server.mjs:7 mounts each resource, '/reports' included (registry.mjs:68), behind authenticate. auth.mjs:29 sets req.user from an HMAC-verified token, so m2 is a real lower-trust caller with tenantId t2 and role manager (users.mjs:5). In reports.mjs:11-16, PUT /:id calls raw store.get(req.params.id), not loadScoped (scoped.mjs:1-7, the tenantId check that GET /:id and DELETE use). Its only authorization is line 14: `item.ownerId !== req.user.id && req.user.role !== 'manager'`, which passes for any manager whatever the tenant. Line 15 then overwrites item.title in the shared in-memory store and line 16 returns the whole item. No other control is on the path: router.mjs only parses the URL and JSON body, routes() only matches method and path, and there is no global tenant middleware. This breaks the README rule that a report may be edited only by its owner or a manager of the same tenant. Impact is limited to what the source shows: a t2 manager can change the title of a t1 report whose id they know, and the response discloses that report's fields. Ids are not enumerable through GET /, which filters by tenant. Caveat: nothing in this repo ever writes to the reports store. There is no POST and no seed, the same as several other resources in this fixture, so the attack assumes a t1 report exists at runtime, which is a normal data-state assumption for an access-control bug.

a47ee2f5.reason: The trace locations exist and match the description. DELETE /reports/:id (reports.mjs:18-22) runs only loadScoped, which is a tenant check (scoped.mjs:1-7). PUT (reports.mjs:14) also checks owner or manager. Authentication is applied to every mount (server.mjs:7, auth.mjs:26-32). So as written, a same-tenant member who is neither owner nor manager is not blocked from deleting. The claimed effect still cannot happen, because the 'reports' store is never populated anywhere in source. reports.mjs defines only GET /, GET /:id, PUT /:id and DELETE /:id, with no POST/create route. storeFor('reports') is a process-local in-memory Map (store.mjs:1-6) that only reports.mjs obtains. No module calls store.set on it, and nothing seeds it (users.mjs seeds only users). Unlike the resources at line 14 of leads/documents/budgets/etc., reports has no creation path, and no report object with an ownerId is ever constructed. Every DELETE therefore reaches loadScoped with store.get(id) returning undefined and throws 404, so there is no other user's report to delete. The prerequisite (an existing report owned by another user) is impossible from the visible source, and the meaningful impact is missing. The README scope question (whether 'edited' covers deletion) does not matter given this. It would only become relevant if a report-creation path existed, and in this in-memory design that would require a code change, not an outside fact.

items.reason: Both list and GET compare against req.user.tenantId, which comes from the server-side users map. Not attacker controlled.

items.title: Session token forgery / claim tampering
items.boundary: unauthenticated client -> HMAC verification -> any user identity
items.reason: The body is HMAC-SHA256 signed and compared with a length check plus timingSafeEqual before parsing, and exp is enforced. sub must exist in the users map. Forging requires SESSION_SECRET.

items.title: Generic CRUD resources cross-tenant access
items.boundary: tenant A user -> loadScoped tenant check -> tenant B records
items.reason: Each of the 30 templated resources filters its list by tenant and calls loadScoped on GET/PUT/DELETE. POST derives tenantId and ownerId from req.user. I verified the group members are identical after normalizing the resource name.

hardening: SESSION_SECRET falls back to a per-process random value (auth.mjs:4): tokens break on restart and cannot be shared between instances. Require it to be set explicitly.
The request body (up to 1MB) is read and parsed before authenticate runs (router.mjs:18), so unauthenticated clients can force parsing work.
A JSON body that parses to null or a primitive makes req.body.<field> throw a TypeError, which becomes a 500. Validate that the body is an object.
verify() calls JSON.parse on the token body without a try/catch. Only a validly signed body reaches that point, so it is not exploitable, but a defensive guard is cheap.
The unmounted legacy-exports.mjs contains an unscoped handler. Remove it or scope it so a future registry change does not expose it.
Tests cover loadScoped only. Add handler-level tests for tenant isolation on invoices, reports and attachments.
Tokens carry no revocation or user-state check beyond the user existing in the map.
